title: Iran war spreads through region as Trump seeks way out
summary: Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue different objectives while searching for a way to end the Iran war.

image.caption: In addition to the Strait of Hormuz, the fighting is now affecting Saudi oil exports through the Red SeaImage: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: Nearly seven months into the Iran war, negotiations between Washington and Tehran have led nowhere, and the conflict has spread from the Strait of Hormuz to another strategically important shipping route.

In September, Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen took over critical positions on the Yemeni coast and are threatening Red Sea trade routes while launching attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia. This compounds a global energy crunch brought on by the Strait of Hormuz blockade.
Earlier in September, Saudi officials blamed Iran-backed militias in Iraq for blowing up the critical East-West oil pipeline.
According to The New York Times, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called US President Donald Trump on Sunday to once again urge him to intervene and stop the Houthi's rapid advance.

Trump is reported to have considered airstrikes against the Houthis at one point, but later abandoned the plans. This weekend, Fox News reported that Trump said the Houthi rebels had agreed not to attack US targets. The US news outlet Axios also reported that Trump had rejected a Saudi request for strikes against the Houthis the previous week.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?

Against the backdrop of record high gasoline and diesel prices coming down hard on voters ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections, US President Donald Trump is under pressure to show results in the Iran war.

"President Trump wants to end the Iran war from a position that allows him to claim that Iran's nuclear and military capabilities have been significantly weakened, freedom of navigation has been restored, and Tehran has been forced back to the negotiating table," Iran expert Fatemeh Aman told DW.

Aman, who has worked with organizations including the Middle East Institute, the Atlantic Council, RFE/RL and Voice of America, however, added that a coherent strategy for achieving these objectives remains difficult to discern.

The US has imposed high military and economic costs on Iran and appears to have made progress in weakening the country's military capabilities. But Tehran has not capitulated and there is no lasting ceasefire agreement.

Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington this week. China is by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil and an important political partner of Tehran. The US president is likely to bring up China's economic and financial ties with Iran and hope that Beijing will use its influence over Tehran — particularly when it comes to the security of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, Trump has signaled that he is open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is traveling to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. Senior representatives from the Gulf states are also expected in the US over the coming days.
According to Axios, Trump plans to discuss the Iran war with representatives of several Gulf states on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Houthi gains in Yemen threaten key Red Sea shipping route
Gulf nations want regional stability

There is still no common position emerging between Iran and its Arab neighbors in the Gulf. A planned meeting involving Iran, the Gulf states and Iraq was canceled last week. The cancellation may be linked to the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.

"At first glance, there appears to be little common ground between Iran and the Gulf states," Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told DW. "But behind the scenes, there is at least a shared interest in preventing further military escalation."
The Gulf states recognize that they would be unlikely to prevail in a direct military confrontation with Iran, and generally favor de-escalation and a pragmatic easing of tensions with Tehran.
An agreement, however, is not currently in sight. In particular, Iran's demands for greater control over the Strait of Hormuz go too far from the perspective of the Gulf states.
The war in Yemen further limits the scope for rapprochement. Saudi Arabia, for example, is unlikely to make concessions while it remains under pressure from the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
Iran's two-track strategy
A permanently hostile, US-backed coalition of Gulf states would be strategically costly for Tehran, Aman said.

She added Iran could pursue a two-track strategy: This would involve resisting a US-led regional containment architecture, while simultaneously offering the Gulf states an alternative model of regional security based on accommodation and dialogue.
"After all, the Gulf states are not only Iran's rivals but also its neighbors — and neither side can change that geographic reality," Aman said.
According to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei, Tehran is demanding that the US end the fighting on all fronts.

Tehran is also calling for the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets and the lifting of the naval blockade in the strait. Talks with Qatar and Oman are reportedly continuing. The Iranian regime is now waiting for a response from Trump. Whether these diplomatic signals can translate into a broader political process remains uncertain.
For now, the main obstacle is that Washington, Tehran and the Gulf states continue to pursue very different roadmaps for ending the months-long conflict.
This article was translated from German.
